name: Regular Expressions
description: Syntax, greediness, groups, lookaround and the catastrophic backtracking that turns a regex into a denial of service.

modules.name: Syntax & Semantics
modules.description: The constructs that make up 95% of real regular expressions.

cards.prompt: What do `*`, `+`, `?`, `{n,m}` mean, and what does adding `?` after them do?
cards.answer: Zero or more, one or more, zero or one, and between n and m repetitions. A trailing `?` makes the quantifier lazy — it matches as little as possible instead of as much.
cards.explanation: `<.*>` on `<a><b>` matches the whole string because `*` is greedy; `<.*?>` matches just `<a>`. Lazy quantifiers are usually the fix when a pattern 'matches too much', though a negated character class `<[^>]*>` is faster still.

cards.code:
import re
s = '<a><b>'
print(re.match(r'<.*>', s).group())
print(re.match(r'<.*?>', s).group())
cards.explanation: Greedy `.*` consumes to the end then backtracks until the final `>` matches. Lazy `.*?` consumes as little as possible and stops at the first `>`. Same pattern shape, completely different result.

cards.prompt: `^` anchors to the start, `$` to the end, and `\___` matches a word boundary.
cards.explanation: In multiline mode `^`/`$` match at every line break — a frequent source of validation bypasses, since `^\d+$` can match `123\nrm -rf /` in some engines. Use `\A` and `\z` where available for absolute string anchors.

cards.answer: Both group for alternation and quantifiers; only capturing groups store the matched text for later reference.

left.title: ( ) capturing
points: Named form `(?<year>...)` is far more readable

cards.explanation: Use named groups for anything you extract — `(?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})` survives someone inserting a group at the front, where `$1`/`$2` silently break.

cards.prompt: What are the four lookaround assertions?
cards.answer: `(?=...)` positive lookahead, `(?!...)` negative lookahead, `(?<=...)` positive lookbehind, `(?<!...)` negative lookbehind. All are zero-width: they assert without consuming characters.
cards.explanation: Classic use: password rules — `^(?=.*[a-z])(?=.*\d).{8,}$` asserts several independent conditions at position 0. Lookbehind support varies (JavaScript gained it in ES2018; some engines require fixed width).

modules.name: Performance & Judgement
modules.description: ReDoS, engine differences, and knowing when not to use a regex at all.

cards.prompt: Why can this pattern hang the process on a 30-character input?
cards.answer: Catastrophic backtracking. Nested quantifiers over overlapping alternatives give exponentially many ways to split the input, and a failing match tries them all — O(2ⁿ).
cards.explanation: This is ReDoS (CWE-1333) and has taken down real services, including a Cloudflare outage in 2019. Avoid nested quantifiers over overlapping patterns, use possessive quantifiers or atomic groups where supported, or use a linear-time engine such as RE2.

resources.title: OWASP — Regular expression denial of service

cards.answer: Backtracking engines (PCRE, Python re, JavaScript) support backreferences and lookaround but can go exponential; automata engines (RE2, Go regexp, rust regex) guarantee linear time by giving those features up.

left.title: Backtracking
points: Needs a timeout on untrusted patterns

cards.explanation: If untrusted input or untrusted patterns are involved, choose the linear engine or impose a hard timeout. Thompson's construction is the theory: a true regular language needs no backtracking.

resources.title: Russ Cox — Regular expression matching can be simple and fast

cards.prompt: When should you *not* reach for a regex?
cards.answer: For nested or recursive structures — HTML, JSON, source code, balanced brackets. Regular languages cannot count nesting; use a real parser.
cards.explanation: Also avoid them for email validation (RFC 5322 is absurd — check for an `@` and send a confirmation), and for anything a string method does more clearly. A regex that needs a comment block to explain it usually wants to be a small parser.

resources.title: Stack Overflow — You can't parse HTML with regex

cards.prompt: Matching complexity of a well-formed regex on a linear-time engine vs a backtracking engine?
cards.answer: O(n·m) on an automata engine (n = input length, m = pattern size); potentially O(2ⁿ) on a backtracking engine.

complexity.time: O(n·m) linear engine; up to O(2ⁿ) backtracking

cards.explanation: Most patterns behave fine on backtracking engines — the danger is specific shapes with nested or ambiguous quantifiers. Compile patterns once outside hot loops; recompiling a regex per iteration is a common and silly cost.

modules.name: Classes, Flags & Replacement
modules.description: Character classes, escaping, flags, backreferences, substitution, splitting and Unicode.

cards.answer: `\d` a digit, `\w` a word character (letter, digit, underscore), `\s` whitespace; the capital versions negate them. `.` matches any character except newline (unless the dotall flag is set). `[abc]` matches one listed character, `[^abc]` any character not listed, and `[a-z]` a range.
cards.explanation: In Unicode-aware engines `\d` and `\w` match far more than ASCII — Python 3 `\d` matches Arabic-Indic digits too. Use `[0-9]` (or the ASCII flag) when you mean ASCII digits, for example when validating input you will pass to `int()`.

cards.prompt: This should match the literal filename, but it also matches `reportXcsv`. Why?
cards.answer: `.` is a metacharacter matching any character. Escape it (`report\.csv`) — and when building a pattern from user input, always escape it with `re.escape()` or its equivalent, otherwise the input can change the pattern's meaning or trigger catastrophic backtracking.
cards.explanation: Metacharacters needing escapes: `. ^ $ * + ? { } [ ] \ | ( )`. Use raw strings in Python (`r"\d+"`) so backslashes reach the regex engine intact. Unescaped user input in a regex is an injection bug, just like unescaped input in SQL.

cards.prompt: What do the common flags `i`, `m`, `s`, `g` and `x` do?
cards.answer: `i` case-insensitive; `m` multiline — `^` and `$` match at every line; `s` dotall — `.` also matches newlines; `g` global — find all matches (JavaScript); `x` verbose — whitespace and `#` comments inside the pattern are ignored, so complex patterns can be laid out readably.
cards.explanation: Verbose mode is the cheapest readability upgrade for any pattern longer than a line. In JavaScript, a `g` regex used with `test()` or `exec()` is stateful via `lastIndex` — reusing one across calls gives alternating true/false results.

In a replacement, `\1` (or `\g<name>`, `$1` in JavaScript) inserts what a group captured, so groups can be reordered. Inside a pattern, a backreference such as `\1` matches the same text again — `\b(\w+) \1\b` finds doubled words. Backreferences are exactly the feature linear-time engines give up.

cards.code:
import re
print(re.findall(r'\d+', 'pi is 3.14159'))
print(re.findall(r'(\w)=(\d)', 'a=1, b=2'))
print(re.split(r'[,;\s]+', 'a, b;c  d'))
cards.explanation: `findall` returns every match; with capturing groups it returns the groups instead of the whole match — tuples when there are several. `split` on a pattern handles multiple delimiters at once. Use `finditer` for large inputs to get match objects lazily, with positions.

cards.answer: `match` anchors at the start of the string only; `search` finds the first match anywhere; `fullmatch` requires the entire string to match.

right.title: search
points: First match anywhere in the string
Returns a match object or None

cards.explanation: Validation should use `fullmatch` (or explicit `^...$`, remembering `$` also matches before a trailing newline in Python). Using `match` to validate lets trailing junk through: `re.match(r"\d+", "123abc")` succeeds.

resources.title: Python docs — re: search() vs match()

cards.prompt: Your name-validation regex `^[A-Za-z]+$` rejects "José" and "Łukasz". How should it change?
cards.answer: Use Unicode properties: `^\p{L}+$` matches letters in any script (JavaScript needs the `u` or `v` flag; Python needs the third-party `regex` module). Better still, reconsider validating names at all beyond length and control characters.
cards.explanation: Real names include spaces, hyphens, apostrophes and characters from every script, and some people have one name only. Overly strict validation is a common and avoidable exclusion bug. Normalise to NFC before matching so composed and decomposed forms behave the same.

cards.prompt: How do you keep a non-trivial regex correct and maintainable?
cards.answer: Write it in verbose mode with comments, give groups names, and unit-test it with a table of inputs that must match and inputs that must not — including edge cases such as empty strings, very long inputs and near-misses. Use an explainer tool (regex101) while developing.
cards.explanation: Tests are what let you change a regex later without fear. Add a pathological long input to check it finishes quickly; if a pattern keeps growing, replace it with a small parser.
